morningLine: This week: the IBM PC reaches its first birthday, August magazines put new home machines and software on the rack, computer-store math still belongs to peripherals, and August 13 crowds the movie marquee.

lead.headline: IBM PC Turns One With the Clone Question Already in the Room
lead.summary: Thursday, August 12 marks one year since IBM announced the Personal Computer. The first-birthday story is not cake; it is compatibility. Buyers now weigh a real IBM 5150 desk against cheaper workalikes, add-in cards, DOS disks, printers, monitors, and the growing office-software shelf. IBM opened the door with a low-cost system built from a system unit, keyboard, diskette drives, monochrome display, and printer options; by this summer, the question on the sales floor is which programs and boards will behave like they belong together.

computerItems.label: IBM PC / compatibles
computerItems.headline: The Birthday Is Also a Compatibility Test
computerItems.summary: A year after IBM's announcement, a shopper is no longer just choosing a box. The practical questions are DOS version, floppy format, display choice, printer speed, add-in cards, and whether the program on the shelf expects true IBM behavior.

computerItems.label: Commodore 64
computerItems.headline: C64 Watch Moves From Showpiece to Store Counter
computerItems.summary: The August launch window remains the home-computer counterweight to IBM's office desk: 64K memory, color, sound, TV hookup, and a $595 list price that keeps Atari, TI, Apple, and Radio Shack salesmen alert.

computerItems.label: Magazine rack
computerItems.headline: Compute! Runs the New Wave Across Its August Rack
computerItems.summary: The August Compute! issue promises an in-depth look at the new Commodore 64, Sinclair Color Spectrum, Epson portable, and more. The table of contents pairs hardware first looks with modem, RS-232, Atari, VIC, and Apple utility material.

computerItems.label: Printers & disks
computerItems.headline: The Peripheral Bill Is Still the Real Bill
computerItems.summary: Retail advertising in the August Compute! issue lists Atari 810 disk drives at $599.95, Epson MX-80 printers at $645, Commodore 2031 single disk drives at $695, and serious daisy-wheel printers above $1,800.
computerItems.confidence: Prices from August 1982 magazine ad text

computerItems.label: Timex / Sinclair
computerItems.headline: Under-$100 BASIC Keeps Pulling Newcomers Toward the Counter
computerItems.summary: The Timex Sinclair 1000 had just arrived through mass retail in July at $99.95. In this issue week it functions as the budget-computer argument beside pricier color machines and office PCs.
computerItems.confidence: Recent July 1982 launch coverage; used as current shelf context

market.headline: Computer Store Market: One Desk, Many Add-Ons
market.summary: This issue skips securities-market filler. The market signal is at retail: the PC birthday brings demand for compatible software and boards, while August magazine ads show printers, disk drives, modems, and word processors pushing the real cost far beyond the headline computer price.

bbsNote.headline: Choosing a Modem Is Now a Department, Not a Footnote
bbsNote.summary: Compute! keeps telecommunications in the magazine stack with modem and RS-232 coverage. The home user still has to reckon with 300-baud patience, telephone bills, and which serial interface belongs on which machine.

posts.text: August Compute! carries VIC communications and RS-232 material for readers pushing beyond cassette-and-cartridge use.
SoftCard and CP/M ads make the Apple feel like two machines at once for software hunters.
The anniversary question: which clone, card, disk, printer, and DOS combination behaves when the office program starts?

curiosity.headline: Friday the 13th Brings a Crowded Marquee
curiosity.summary: August 13 sends Fast Times at Ridgemont High, Friday the 13th Part 3, The Soldier, Star Wars in re-release, and Tempest into wide release listings. The office computer may be turning one, but the weekend ticket line is pure late-summer 1982.
